understanding.purpose: Inventory servers by host, role, zone, CPU, status, and operational notes.
understanding.reading: Readers scan hosts and compare roles, locations, CPU counts, and health; the single long note explains an exception and can occupy a taller row.
groups: Host and Role identify each server and its function.
Zone and CPU describe placement and capacity.
Status and Notes pair health with operational context.
may_wrap: The long operational note at natural word boundaries
Zone identifiers at hyphens if more space is needed for the note

bad.why: Every zone identifier breaks across three lines, making a frequently compared field harder to scan and greatly enlarging otherwise sparse rows.
The CPU header breaks inside the abbreviation, weakening the header hierarchy to save one line in a single note.
Every zone identifier wraps, making comparisons harder and adding height to nearly every row for a small gain in the one long note.

final.rationale: The preferred designs keep hosts, roles, zones, CPU values and statuses intact, so each server can be scanned across a compact row. They give the exceptional note the remaining width, accepting a taller row where the extra space is needed. r0B is still readable, though its wider short-value columns leave less room for the note.

general: Protect the integrity of repeated identifiers and headers that readers use to scan and compare rows.
Allocate width according to content and reading purpose; wrapping prose can be preferable to wrapping short categorical values.
specific: Only one server has a long note, so its tall row is less disruptive than wrapping the zone in every row.
r0A and r1A have identical widths and render identically.

final.tradeoffs: A wider note can reduce the height of the exceptional row, but taking that space from Zone or CPU damages fields used throughout the table. r0B gives the short columns more breathing room at the cost of an extra line in the note.
final.uncertain: The ranges are conservative estimates around the preferred widths, not independently rendered thresholds. They assume proportional adjustment of the other columns within the 719px limit; exact equivalence depends on browser wrapping and rounding.

A.why: Zone identifiers wrap onto three lines throughout, and some host names split; the wide Notes column does not compensate for the damage to scanning the inventory.

B.why: The narrow Notes column turns the one substantial note into a very tall, fragmented row, while the other columns have space to spare.

C.why: Host names and zones stay intact, compact fields have enough room, and Notes has a comfortable measure. The rows remain easy to scan and compare.

D.why: Identifiers stay intact and the table scans cleanly, though extra space in the short fields leaves the note narrower and its row taller than in C.

E.why: Host names stay intact, but every zone identifier wraps onto three lines, making otherwise sparse rows unnecessarily tall and harder to compare.

A.why: Every zone identifier breaks across three lines, making routine rows tall and hindering comparison, while the notes column has ample space.

B.why: Identifiers stay intact and the ordinary rows are compact. The relatively narrow notes column makes the degraded row taller than necessary.

C.why: All identifiers stay intact, routine rows are compact, and the notes have enough width to read comfortably without unduly widening the other columns.

D.why: Zone identifiers break across three lines, and some host names also split, making the inventory harder to scan and compare.

E.why: The narrow notes column turns one entry into a long, fragmented block and splits a host reference, while short fields receive excessive space.

reviews.unsure: The relative importance of keeping the incident note compact versus giving the inventory fields extra breathing room is not specified.
